A lot more.

Don Layman's math: with 100% animal protein, under 40 grams a day meets your essential amino acid requirements. Go vegetarian or vegan and, in his words, "you're going to be approaching 120 to 130 grams of protein probably."

People who go plant-based tend to lean on grains, he says. Beans and lentils make up only about 18% of plant-based protein, and the rest comes from "very poor quality" grains.

nuevos.titulo_original: What the Astaxanthin Skin Trials Found
nuevos.descripcion:
A lot of people now take astaxanthin, the red pigment in salmon, for their skin. So what do the human trials show?

On sunburn, I could find one small study from 2018, with 22 people, run by employees of the company that funded it. By the end, both groups needed about the same dose of ultraviolet (UV) light before their skin reddened. But compared with placebo, the astaxanthin group's threshold rose significantly more from where it started.

When the small skin trials were pooled in 2021, covering about 300 people, moisture and elasticity seemed to improve, but wrinkles didn't change significantly. The authors called the findings preliminary and noted that several trials were run or funded by companies.

After looking at the research, I don't think astaxanthin is worth paying for to help your skin. The benefits look very small or nonexistent.

Can rapamycin reverse skin aging?

In this episode of Longevity Science, I sit down with Dr. Chris Sell and Dr. Christina Chung, co-founders of Hayflick Therapeutics, to explore the science behind using rapamycin to target aging in the skin.

Chris has spent decades studying cellular senescence, IGF signaling, mTOR, and rapamycin. Christina is a dermatologist whose work with transplant patients gave her a very different perspective on rapamycin and its effects on skin biology. Their paths eventually converged around a fascinating question: could targeting mTOR with topical rapamycin actually improve the function and appearance of aging human skin?

We discuss the early experiments showing that rapamycin can extend the replicative lifespan of human cells, what happens when mTOR remains active in senescent cells, and how Chris and Christina moved from basic science to a controlled human study of topical rapamycin. 

We also talk about why skin may be an underappreciated organ in geroscience, the difference between scientifically rigorous skin rejuvenation and the enormous amount of hype in the aesthetics industry, and why Hayflick is pursuing the much more difficult path of FDA approval.

More broadly, this conversation gets at one of the biggest challenges facing geroscience: how do we translate interventions that affect fundamental mechanisms of aging into therapies that can actually be tested, approved, and used
